issues.legal_issue: A successive application for leave in the same proceeding is not barred by res judicata when the earlier application was disposed of without adjudicating its merits.
material_facts: An earlier application sought leave in connection with eviction proceedings involving a company in liquidation.

The earlier application was disposed of after the opposing party stated that it would not oppose an application to amend a pending suit; the court said it was unnecessary to grant the application then and reserved liberty to apply if necessary.
The earlier order did not decide on the merits whether leave should be granted.
A later application seeking leave for eviction proceedings was granted, but the appellate court set that order aside on the ground that the earlier order operated as res judicata.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order did not operate as res judicata because the leave issue had not been adjudicated on its merits; the later application was therefore not barred.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata may apply between successive stages of the same litigation, but only where the issue was actually decided earlier, with a conscious adjudication and an expression of an opinion on the merits. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi, Arjun Singh v. Mohindra Kumar, Prahlad Singh v. Col. Sukhdev Singh, C.V. Rajendran v. N.M. Muhammed Kunhi, and Y.B. Patil v. Y.L. Patil. It distinguished Kewal Chand Mimani v. S.K. Sen, explaining that the meaning of a reservation of liberty depends on its context and that a reservation following no decision on the merits does not have the same effect as liberty following a final adjudication.

predicates.successive_application_in_same_proceedin: A party files a later application in the same proceeding seeking relief that was the subject of an earlier application.
predicates.earlier_application_disposed_without_mer: The court disposes of the earlier application without deciding the requested relief on its merits.

issues.definition: When a later application in the same proceeding follows an earlier application that was disposed of without a decision on the merits, the later application is not barred by res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: Leave to commence or continue a proceeding against a company in liquidation may be obtained after the proceeding has begun.
material_facts: A company had been ordered to be wound up.
Eviction proceedings involving the company were instituted or proposed, and an application was made to the winding-up court for leave in connection with those proceedings.
An objection was raised that leave had to be obtained before institution of the proceeding.
issues.conclusion: Leave is not a condition precedent to commencing a proceeding against a company in liquidation and may be obtained after the proceeding has begun.
issues.legal_principle: Section 446(1) of the Companies Act, 1956 requires leave for a suit or other legal proceeding against a company in liquidation but does not provide that a proceeding begun without prior leave is annulled or that subsequent leave cannot be granted. The Court relied on Central Bank of India v. Elmot Engineering Company, Ammonia Supplies Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Modern Plastic Containers Pvt. Ltd., State of J&K v. UCO Bank, and Bansidhar Shankarlal v. Mohd. Ibrahim. The provision protects the company's interests and assets from unnecessary litigation and expense; the winding-up court has discretion whether to grant leave and on what conditions. The Court noted that a proceeding may be regarded as instituted on the date leave is obtained.

predicates.proceeding_against_company_in_winding_up: A party commences or seeks to continue a legal proceeding against a company after the company has entered winding up.
predicates.leave_sought_after_commencement: The party seeks the winding-up court's permission after the legal proceeding has begun.

issues.definition: When a legal proceeding against a company in winding up has begun before permission is sought, the court may still grant permission afterward.
